Ask a finance team where they want to start with AI and you will usually
hear one of three answers: variance commentary, board paper summarising,
or "the audit file". These are the three most interesting problems in the
room. They are also, on any honest assessment, three of the worst places
to begin.

The reason is not that the work is too hard. It is that in all three
cases you cannot cheaply tell whether the output is right. A draft that
sounds like a competent colleague wrote it, and is wrong in one place you
did not look, costs you more than doing the job yourself. You pay twice:
once for the draft, once for the review that has to be as careful as the
original work.

What follows is a way of choosing that does not rely on anyone's
enthusiasm: five factors, scored one to five, applied to the tasks your
team actually does. It takes forty-five minutes with the right people in
a room, and it produces two starter use cases you can defend to a
sceptic, plus a written reason for everything you left out.

## Part One — The five-factor score

Score every candidate task on five factors, one to five. Total out of
twenty-five. Two of the factors are inverted, which matters — read the
definitions before you score anything.

### Factor 1 — Frequency

How often does this task recur?

| Score | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| 1 | Once a year or less. A one-off. |
| 2 | A few times a year. Quarterly. |
| 3 | Monthly. |
| 4 | Weekly, or several times a month. |
| 5 | Daily, or many times a day. |

Frequency is where the money is. A task that takes an hour and happens
once a year is worth an hour a year. The same task done weekly is worth
fifty. Teams routinely pick the annual monster over the weekly
irritation, because the monster is memorable and the irritation is
invisible.

One exception, and it is a real one. Some low-frequency tasks produce an
artefact that then gets used constantly — a close checklist, a set of KPI
definitions, a process note. Score the *task* honestly at 1 and note the
durable output separately. A 1 with a permanent artefact behind it is a
legitimate reason to promote a task up the list. A 1 with a disposable
output is not.

### Factor 2 — Time

How long does one instance take now, done by the person who normally does
it?

| Score | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| 1 | Under ten minutes. |
| 2 | Ten to thirty minutes. |
| 3 | Half an hour to two hours. |
| 4 | Half a day to a full day. |
| 5 | More than a day. |

Score the time it takes *now*, not the time you imagine it should take.
If nobody knows, time three instances before the meeting. Guessing here
corrupts everything downstream, because time and frequency together are
the only two factors that describe the prize. The other three describe
the cost of collecting it.

Do not score the time you think the tool will save. You do not know that
yet, and the point of the exercise is to stop deciding on things you do
not know.

### Factor 3 — Verifiability

How easily can you tell whether the output is right?

| Score | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| 1 | You cannot tell without redoing the work from scratch, or correctness is a judgement no one available can make quickly. |
| 2 | Checking takes nearly as long as doing. Errors are plausible and quiet. |
| 3 | Checkable, but only by someone who knows the subject, reading the whole thing. |
| 4 | A knowledgeable person spots an error quickly — minutes, not hours. |
| 5 | Correctness is mechanical and obvious. It ties, it foots, it matches the ledger, or the sheet returns the answer you already knew. |

This is the factor teams overscore, every time, because verification
feels like an afterthought rather than part of the work. It is not an
afterthought. It is the entire economics of the thing.

Write the verifiability score last, and write it as a sentence first:
"I would know this was wrong because ______." If you cannot finish that
sentence in one breath, the score is 1 or 2. If the sentence is "because
I would read it carefully", that is a 2 or a 3, not a 5 — careful reading
is exactly the expensive thing you were trying to avoid.

### Factor 4 — Consequence of error — inverted

If a mistake gets through, what happens? **High score means cheap
mistake.** This factor runs backwards on purpose, so that every factor
points the same way and the total means something.

| Score | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| 1 | The error reaches a client, a regulator, a lender, a court or a board, or a professional duty attaches to the work. Expensive and slow to unwind. |
| 2 | The error reaches someone outside your team and has to be corrected formally. Embarrassing. |
| 3 | The error flows into something else — a return, a report, a system — and gets found later, out of context. |
| 4 | The error is caught in normal internal review. Costs minutes and some grumbling. |
| 5 | The error is caught instantly by the person who asked, and nobody outside the room ever knows. |

Score the consequence of the error *escaping*, not of it being made.
Everything gets reviewed in theory. Ask what happens on a Friday
afternoon in a busy week.

### Factor 5 — Data sensitivity — inverted

What has to go into the tool for the task to work? **High score means
nothing confidential.** Also inverted.

| Score | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| 1 | Impossible without named personal data, client confidential material, unpublished price-sensitive information, or credentials. |
| 2 | Real internal records — ledger detail, supplier and customer names, transaction data. |
| 3 | Internal material that identifies your organisation and its people, but no client data and nothing price-sensitive. |
| 4 | Internal but generic. Procedures, structures, definitions. |
| 5 | Nothing confidential at all. Public, generic, or fully anonymised without effort. |

Two practical notes. First, "we would anonymise it" only counts if
anonymising is quick and reliable. Twenty minutes of careful redaction
per instance belongs in the Time score, and the task is less attractive
than it looked.

Second, this is general information and not legal advice. What you may
put into which tool depends on your contracts with clients, your own
confidentiality obligations, the rules of your professional body and the
data protection law where you and your clients sit. Those differ by
jurisdiction and they change. Get your own position checked rather than
relying on a score in a table.

### Reading the total

| Total | Reading |
|---|---|
| 20–25 | Start here. Rare. If you have one, do it this month. |
| 16–19 | The working middle. Most of a sensible programme lives in this band. |
| 11–15 | Conditional. Worth doing only if you can redesign the task to lift the weak factor. |
| 10 or below | Leave it. Revisit in a year if something changes. |

Then apply three vetoes, which override the total completely:

1. **Verifiability of 1 or 2 — vetoed.** Whatever the total.
2. **Consequence of 1 — vetoed.** Whatever the total.
3. **Data sensitivity of 1 — vetoed.** Whatever the total.

A data sensitivity of 2 is not a veto but a constraint: that task is only
available to you inside a tool where the material genuinely stays under
your control, on terms someone has actually read. If you do not have such
a tool, every 2 behaves like a 1 and drops out.

The vetoes exist because a total is an average, and averages hide the one
thing that will hurt you. A task scoring 4, 5, 2, 1, 1 — frequent, slow,
unverifiable, catastrophic if wrong, full of client data — totals 13 and
sits comfortably mid-range. Thirteen out of twenty-five is not a
comfortable task. It is a disaster with good attendance.

### Why the "time" trap catches everyone

Here is the failure mode this whole method exists to prevent.

Someone proposes a task that scores 4 or 5 on time. It is the task that
eats their Thursday. It is genuinely painful and everybody agrees it is
painful, which makes it feel like an obvious candidate. But it scores 2
on verifiability, because the only way to know the output is right is to
do the underlying work.

The arithmetic is brutal. The task takes four hours; the tool drafts it
in ten minutes. You have not saved three hours and fifty minutes. You
have saved nothing until the draft is checked, and checking an
unverifiable four-hour output takes close to four hours, because the
check *is* the work. You have added ten minutes and a false sense of
progress.

Worse, the draft is persuasive. It is fluent, well-structured and
confident. A checker reading a fluent draft looks for errors; a person
doing the work from scratch encounters the facts. Those are different
mental activities and they catch different things. A fluent wrong draft
is harder to correct than a blank page, because it tells you where to
look and the place it tells you to look is not where the error is.

So: **time tells you the size of the prize; verifiability tells you
whether you can collect it.** A high time score with a low verifiability
score is not a good use case with a snag. It is a bad use case that looks
good, which is worse than one that looks bad, because someone will
champion it.

The corollary is cheering. Tasks that score modestly on time — twenty
minutes, done daily, checked in ten seconds — are the ones that quietly
pay. They are unglamorous, nobody will present them at a conference, and
they will save your team more hours this year than the Thursday monster
ever will.

## Part Two — Thirty tasks, scored

Below are thirty tasks common to finance functions and professional
firms, scored against the five factors. The scores are mine and they are
arguable — deliberately so. The point of a published scale is that you
can look at a row, disagree with one number, and see exactly which
definition we read differently. Change the score, change the total, carry
on. What you must not do is change a score because you want a different
answer.

Assume a general-purpose assistant of the kind anyone can reach from a
browser. Where a row is constrained by data sensitivity, the constraint
means an enterprise-tier arrangement your organisation controls, on terms
someone has read.

Key: **F** frequency, **T** time, **V** verifiability, **C** consequence
(inverted), **D** data sensitivity (inverted).

| # | Task | F | T | V | C | D | Total | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Explaining an inherited spreadsheet formula | 4 | 2 | 5 | 5 | 5 | **21** | Best possible starter — paste the formula, not the data; the sheet marks the answer. |
| 2 | Writing a formula or query from a plain description | 4 | 2 | 5 | 5 | 5 | **21** | Same family. Test on a sample where you know the result before trusting it. |
| 3 | Drafting an internal training exercise for the team | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 5 | **19** | Low risk, genuinely useful. Check the model answers yourself. |
| 4 | Reconciliation prep — formatting and first-pass matching | 5 | 3 | 5 | 4 | 2 | **19** | High frequency and the ledger marks the work. Constrained only by where the data may go. |
| 5 | Meeting notes into circulated minutes | 5 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 3 | **18** | Strong starter. You were in the room, so you can mark the output. |
| 6 | Routine client emails — updates, chasers, acknowledgements | 5 | 1 | 5 | 4 | 3 | **18** | Small saving each time, large in aggregate. Never send unread. |
| 7 | Process documentation for a routine task | 2 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | **18** | High value; the person who does the task is the reviewer. Backlog makes it better than it scores. |
| 8 | Month-end close checklist — build or refresh | 1 | 3 | 5 | 4 | 5 | **18** | One afternoon, permanent artefact. An excellent pilot. |
| 9 | Internal finance policy — first draft | 1 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 5 | **18** | Good use. The draft is a skeleton; the control detail must be yours. |
| 10 | Job description for a finance vacancy | 2 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | **18** | Fine filler task. Do not let it invent qualifications, or say anything about pay you have not decided. |
| 11 | Audit request list / information list for a client | 2 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 5 | **17** | Quick win before every audit. Your auditor will amend it anyway. |
| 12 | Interview questions and scoring sheet for a finance hire | 1 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | **17** | Solid and low-stakes. Keep the scoring criteria yours. |
| 13 | User acceptance test cases for a system or control | 1 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | **17** | Good. The tool supplies breadth; you supply the nasty cases. |
| 14 | KPI definition dictionary | 1 | 3 | 5 | 4 | 4 | **17** | Unglamorous, durable, week-one material. Your team recognises a wrong definition instantly. |
| 15 | Plain-language rewrite of a technical memo | 3 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 3 | **16** | Common and useful. The check is fast because you own the source. |
| 16 | Forecast scenario — building the structure | 2 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 3 | **16** | Use it for scaffolding, never for assumptions. Test the mechanics with known inputs. |
| 17 | Cleaning and standardising a messy data extract | 4 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 2 | **15** | Only with row-count and total controls in place. Silent row loss is the risk, not visible errors. |
| 18 | Invoice coding suggestions against the chart of accounts | 5 | 1 | 4 | 3 | 2 | **15** | Volume is the attraction. Treat every suggestion as a first pass a human approves. |
| 19 | Fixed asset register tidy-up — descriptions and categories | 1 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 3 | **14** | Middle of the pack. Check categories yourself; they drive depreciation and tax. |
| 20 | Long email chain into a decision log | 4 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 2 | **14** | Useful for your own recall. Weak as a record anyone else relies on. |
| 21 | Variance commentary — first draft from figures you supply | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 2 | **14** | The classic trap. Quick to draft, slow to trust — the tool cannot know *why* the number moved. |
| 22 | Contract summarising into a key-terms schedule | 3 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | **13** | **Vetoed** on data. The check is re-reading the contract, which was the work. |
| 23 | Board paper summarising | 2 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 1 | **11** | **Vetoed** on data. The omission you cannot see is the entire risk. |
| 24 | Audit working paper — documenting work performed | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 1 | **11** | **Vetoed** three ways. The record must describe what you actually did. |
| 25 | Tax computation review | 2 | 4 | 2 | 1 | 1 | **10** | **Vetoed.** Use it for the covering memo if anything, never the computation. |
| 26 | Payroll queries involving named individuals | 3 | 2 | 3 | 1 | 1 | **10** | **Vetoed.** Named pay data, and the error lands on a person. |
| 27 | Credit assessment of a named customer | 3 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 1 | **10** | **Vetoed.** A decision about a named party on data you cannot check. |
| 28 | Researching the treatment of a novel transaction | 2 | 4 | 1 | 1 | 2 | **10** | **Vetoed.** Where confident-sounding wrong answers do the most damage. |
| 29 | A difficult client email — bad news, fee dispute, complaint | 2 | 2 | 3 | 1 | 1 | **9** | **Vetoed.** In a live dispute your words become evidence. Write it yourself. |
| 30 | Drafting a response to a regulator or professional body | 1 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 1 | **8** | **Vetoed.** The lowest score here, and rightly. |

### What the table is telling you

Read the shape of it rather than the individual rows.

**The top is boring.** The two highest scores are explaining and writing
spreadsheet formulas — tasks so small that nobody would propose them in a
strategy meeting. They win because the sheet tells you immediately
whether the answer works, and because you paste a formula rather than
data. Frequency and verifiability, not ambition.

**The bottom is everything anyone was excited about.** Board papers, tax
computations, working paper documentation, regulator correspondence.
These are the tasks that hurt most, which is precisely why they involve
the most confidential material and the heaviest consequences. Pain and
suitability are not correlated. If anything they run against each other.

**The middle is where the argument is.** Rows 17 to 21 all score 14 or
15 — data cleaning, invoice coding, variance commentary. These are the
rows worth an hour of your team's disagreement, because the score depends
on facts about your organisation that I do not have. If your ledger data
can sit in a tool you control, invoice coding moves from 15 to 18 and
becomes a serious candidate. If it cannot, it drops out entirely. Same
task, different organisation, different answer.

**Two rows deserve a word each.**

*Variance commentary* (row 21) is the single most requested use case in
finance, and it scores 14. The figures are verifiable; the explanation is
not. A tool can see that distribution costs moved. It cannot know that
you changed courier in week three, and it will not say
"I don't know" — it will produce a plausible reason. Plausible reasons in
management commentary are worse than blank space, because someone will
act on one. If you use a tool here at all, use it to draft the
*structure* and to check that every movement above your threshold has
been addressed. Supply the causes yourself.

*Audit working paper documentation* (row 24) scores 11 and is vetoed
three times over. It deserves the emphasis. A generated narrative
describing work performed is indistinguishable, on the page, from a
narrative describing work performed — whether or not it was. That is not
a technology problem you can solve with a better prompt. It is the reason
the record exists. Where professional duties attach to your file, the
documentation is the evidence of the work, and it has to be written by
the person who did it. Check what your own professional body and your
firm's methodology require; this varies and it changes.

### Disagreeing properly

Someone in your team will say a score is wrong. Good. Handle it like
this:

1. Name the factor. Not "this should be higher" — "verifiability should
   be 4, not 3".
2. Quote the definition. Read the row from the scale out loud.
3. Say what you would do differently. "I would know it was wrong because
   the control total does not match" is an argument for 5. "I would read
   it properly" is not.
4. Change the number and let the total fall where it falls.

The one rule: nobody argues about a total. Totals are arithmetic. If you
find yourself defending a total, you have decided the answer and are
reverse-engineering the scores, and the method has stopped working.

## Part Three — Running this in your own team in forty-five minutes

This is a single meeting. It does not need a workshop, a facilitator or a
wall of sticky notes, and it produces a decision rather than a
discussion.

### Who is in the room

Four to eight people. You need three roles covered, and one person can
cover two:

- **People who do the work.** They score frequency and time. Nobody else
  is entitled to.
- **People who review the work.** They score verifiability and
  consequence. The reviewer's verifiability score wins any tie, because
  they are the one who will pay for a bad one.
- **Whoever owns confidentiality and data protection.** They score data
  sensitivity, and they hold a veto that needs no explanation.

Do not invite anyone whose only contribution is enthusiasm.

### Before the meeting

Circulate the five factor scales — just the five tables from Part One,
one page. Ask everyone to bring **three tasks they personally do**,
written on separate lines, described concretely. "Reporting" is not a
task. "Writing the commentary on the departmental cost report" is.

If nobody knows how long a candidate task takes, ask the person who does
it to time three instances that week. Ten minutes of measurement beats an
hour of estimating, and the number is defensible afterwards.

### The agenda

| Time | Item | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:05 | Purpose and rules. Read out the three vetoes. | Everyone knows a high total can still lose. |
| 0:05–0:12 | Silent listing. Each person writes their three tasks. No discussion. | 12–24 raw candidates. |
| 0:12–0:20 | Read out and merge. Combine duplicates, discard anything nobody actually does. | A clean list of 15–25. |
| 0:20–0:35 | Score. Thirty seconds a task, by role, in order F-T-V-C-D. | Every task has five numbers. |
| 0:35–0:42 | Apply vetoes. Strike the failures. Sort by total. | A ranked, filtered list. |
| 0:42–0:45 | Pick two. Name an owner each. Set the review date. | A decision. |

Fifteen minutes for scoring sounds tight and is not. Thirty seconds a
task is enough when the scales are on the table in front of people, and
the clock is doing useful work: it stops the room relitigating a task
everyone already understands.

### Rules for the room

- **Silent listing first.** Open with discussion and the most senior or
  most talkative person sets the agenda; you will score their three tasks.
- **Score by role, not by consensus.** The doer's time score stands, the
  reviewer's verifiability score stands. Consensus drifts towards
  whatever the room already wanted.
- **No scoring your own task alone.** If you do the task and review it,
  someone else scores verifiability.
- **Write the "I would know it was wrong because ______" sentence out
  loud** for anything scoring 4 or 5 on verifiability. Half of them
  collapse to a 3 the moment they are spoken.
- **Vetoes are silent.** No debate. The veto is not a judgement about the
  task or the person who proposed it.

### What you leave with

Two use cases. Not five, and not one.

One gives you no comparison: if it goes badly you cannot tell whether the
method or the task was at fault. Five gives you five half-started
experiments and no evidence, because no small team learns five new habits
at once.

For each of the two, write down before you leave the room:

1. The owner. One named person, not a team.
2. The baseline: how long the task takes now, measured over three
   instances, and how often it happens.
3. What "working" would look like in four weeks, in time or rework — not
   in enthusiasm.
4. The verification step, in one sentence, written before anyone starts.
5. The date you will look at it again. Four weeks is about right.

### After four weeks

Come back for fifteen minutes. Three possible answers:

- **It worked.** Write down what verification actually cost, because that
  is the number you will need when someone proposes the next task. Then
  score the next two candidates from your ranked list.
- **It half-worked.** Usually this means the verification step was
  invented afterwards rather than designed first. Fix that and run
  another four weeks. Do not widen.
- **It did not work.** Say so plainly, record why against the five
  factors, and move to the next candidate. A use case that fails against
  a written scale is information. A use case that fails against nothing
  is just a bad mood.

### If nothing scores well

This happens, particularly in small practices where nearly everything
touches client confidential material. If your list has no task above 15
and every high scorer is vetoed on data, that is a genuine finding, and
it is worth more than a forced pilot.

It usually points at one of two things. Either your tooling is the
constraint — the work would qualify if the material stayed under your
control, which is a procurement question rather than a use case question.
Or your suitable tasks are all small and you have been looking for
something big. In the second case, go back to the top of the table:
formula explanation, checklists, definitions, internal drafting. Small,
frequent, instantly checkable, nothing confidential. That is not a
consolation prize. On the arithmetic, it is the answer.

### Re-run it

Score again every quarter, or whenever one of three things changes: the
tools available to you, your policy on what data may go where, or the
shape of the work. Keep the old scoresheets. Being able to show why a
task was rejected in March and what changed by September is worth as much
as the decision itself — particularly to whoever has to answer for it.
